title: Freya and the Cellar
premise: Ada Vane returns to the family farmhouse to bury his twin brother Freya, only to find the body in the casket is not Freya at all—and that Freya may never have left the cellar where their father kept him for years. As Ada documents the house's wrongness in a journal, the mirrors begin lagging a second behind reality, and a children's song hummed through the floorboards reveals itself as an invocation that keeps something fed and bound. Ada learns he was meant to be the one in the cellar, swapped out by their mother's bargain, and that the song's last verse can either free the thing below or hand it his name. In the end, Ada sings the verse deliberately but offers the house a substitute—his own documented confession of the family's crimes—binding the entity to truth instead of flesh, though the final mirror still shows him a half-second late, forever.
about_author: Isandro Dunmore is the pen name of a former rural coroner's assistant who spent six years cataloguing unclaimed remains in the American Midwest. Their fiction draws on case files they were never allowed to discuss.

chapters.title: The Wrong Brother
chapters.summary: Ada Vane arrives at the farmhouse for the funeral and lifts the casket lid to find a stranger's face wearing Freya's suit. Told in Ada's close third person, the chapter establishes his compulsive documentation habit as grief management. Emotional beat: cold disbelief hardening into dread.

chapters.title: Inventory of a House
chapters.summary: Ada catalogs every room, photographing details no one asked for, and notices the cellar door has three new locks facing inward. POV stays with Ada; flashbacks sketch Freya as the quiet twin who 'went away to school.' Emotional beat: unease disguised as tidiness.

chapters.title: One Second Late
chapters.summary: Ada catches his reflection raising its hand after he does. He tests every mirror in the house, timing the lag with his phone stopwatch: exactly one second, everywhere. The chapter's horror is procedural and precise. Emotional beat: the scientist's calm beginning to crack.

chapters.title: The Song Under the Floor
chapters.summary: At night Ada hears a child humming through the cellar boards—a lullaby he knows, because their mother sang it. He records it; playback contains a second voice underneath. Emotional beat: nostalgia curdling into recognition.

chapters.title: What the Neighbors Know
chapters.summary: Ada visits elderly neighbor Ruth Calloway, who goes pale at Freya's name and says only: 'Your mother paid for which boy lived.' She slams the door. POV Ada, with Ruth's dialogue carrying the revelation. Emotional beat: first confirmation the horror is human-made.

chapters.title: The Journal of Margaret Vane
chapters.summary: Ada finds his mother's hidden ledger documenting payments, dates, and a recurring entry: 'Verse withheld.' Her handwriting deteriorates across decades. Emotional beat: pity for the mother braided with fury at what she purchased.

chapters.title: Freya's Room, Sealed
chapters.summary: Behind drywall Ada finds a small room with scratch marks, a child's drawings of a 'mirror friend,' and Freya's real belongings. He realizes the 'school' story was cover for confinement. Emotional beat: guilt arriving like a physical blow.

chapters.title: The Lag Grows
chapters.summary: The mirrors are now two seconds behind, and Ada sees reflections doing things he hasn't done yet—pouring tea, opening the cellar door. He stops sleeping. Emotional beat: loss of trust in his own senses.

chapters.title: Ruth's Confession
chapters.summary: Ruth, dying and frightened, tells Ada about the founding families' pact: feed the cellar-thing a child's name each generation or lose the town. The song keeps it docile; the last verse was never taught. Emotional beat: horror of inherited complicity.

chapters.title: Which Twin Was Promised
chapters.summary: Reading Margaret's ledger against birth records, Ada discovers the original bargain named him—but his mother substituted Freya, buying Ada's ordinary life with his brother's captivity. Emotional beat: survivor's guilt detonating into purpose.

chapters.title: Descent, First Attempt
chapters.summary: Ada unlocks the cellar and gets halfway down before the temperature drops and his own recorded voice plays back from the dark, singing the verse slightly wrong. He retreats. Emotional beat: courage measured and found insufficient.

chapters.title: Learning the Song
chapters.summary: Ada transcribes the lullaby from Ruth's memory and old hymnals, reconstructing verses while refusing to sing aloud—the rule being you must know it without offering your voice. Emotional beat: obsessive scholarship as self-protection.

chapters.title: The Town That Looks Away
chapters.summary: In town, Ada confronts descendants of the pact families; they deny everything politely, then slash his tires and leave a hymnal on his hood, open to the lullaby. Emotional beat: isolation—the price of seeing clearly.

chapters.title: Freya Speaks
chapters.summary: Through the lagging mirrors, Ada finally communicates with Freya—not dead, but changed, existing in the reflected second. Freya warns: the thing below wears our faces now, and it wants the last verse sung by blood. Emotional beat: reunion shadowed by unrecognizability.

chapters.title: The Substitute Face
chapters.summary: Ada finds photos proving the body in the casket was a pact-family castoff given Freya's name—a town tradition of disposable dead. His rage turns toward the whole community. Emotional beat: justice becoming personal.

chapters.title: Verse Five of Six
chapters.summary: Ruth dies mid-teaching, leaving Ada five verses and a warning: the sixth must be given freely, never coerced, or the binding fails. The mirrors now lag four seconds. Emotional beat: grief compressing time.

chapters.title: The House Turns
chapters.summary: The farmhouse begins rearranging itself—doors leading to the cellar regardless of direction, walls sweating cold. Ada realizes the house is herding him downward. Emotional beat: claustrophobic surrender of control.

chapters.title: What Waits Below
chapters.summary: Ada descends fully and meets the entity: a composite of every promised child, wearing Freya's face most often because it's closest to true. It offers him a trade—his name for Freya's freedom. Emotional beat: temptation rendered almost reasonable.

chapters.title: The Bargain Refused
chapters.summary: Ada refuses the trade, understanding that any exchange just renews the cycle. The entity begins taking his reflection piece by piece; he is fading from the mirrors even as he stands there. Emotional beat: terror transfigured into resolve.

chapters.title: The Last Verse
chapters.summary: In the cellar, Ada sings the sixth verse—but substitutes the ledger, reading his family's crimes aloud as the offering, binding the entity to memory rather than sacrifice. The house screams. Emotional beat: catharsis through truth-telling.

chapters.title: Aftermath, Documented
chapters.summary: The mirrors clear except one. Freya, freed but not restored, chooses to stay in the reflected second where he is safe; the brothers part through glass. Ada buries the stranger under a nameless marker and burns the pact records—or tries to. Emotional beat: mourning without closure.

chapters.title: One Second Late (Reprise)
chapters.summary: Weeks later, in a city apartment, Ada journals by habit and catches his reflection pausing a beat too long—then nodding, once, deliberately. He understands the binding holds, and that Freya watches. Final line: documentation is a kind of prayer, and someone is listening. Emotional beat: haunted peace.
